cards.headline: 100 animals rescued in Martin County hoarding case west of Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered.
cards.body:
Authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property on Monday. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and five more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs. Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said about 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets. She said every single one of them left in tears because the organization did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets. More identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

hero.headline: Single-family home prices rise across Treasure Coast after two years of declines
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast, with every county in the region seeing an increase in median home sale prices. The increases come after price drops from 2023 to 2025.

Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers. Buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. Condos and townhomes show a different trend, with prices dropping in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increasing by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County food and spirits fundraiser returns to Stuart in October
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties said the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: Florida spiny lobster mini season opens Wednesday with strict two-day harvest window
hero.body:
Florida's spiny lobster sport season returns Wednesday, July 29 through Thursday, July 30, offering recreational divers and snorkelers a two-day opportunity to harvest the prized crustaceans. The annual event occurs on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday of July each year and is open to both Florida residents and non-residents. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission enforces strict bag limits that vary by location, with Monroe County and Biscayne National Park restricted to 6 lobsters per person per day, while the rest of Florida waters allow 12 lobsters per person per day. Possession limits on the water equal the daily bag limit, while off-water possession on July 29 equals the daily bag limit and doubles on July 30 to either 12 or 24 depending on location.

All harvested spiny lobsters must meet Florida's minimum size requirement, with carapace length exceeding 3 inches when measured in water. Possession and use of an approved measuring device is mandatory at all times, and all measurements must be taken while the lobster is still in the water. Night diving is prohibited in Monroe County during the sport season only, with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission defining diving as swimming at or below the water surface. This restriction applies exclusively to Monroe County waters during the July 29-30 sport season.

Several areas remain completely off-limits to lobster harvesting, including John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary no-take zones, Biscayne Bay/Card Sound Lobster Sanctuary, and five Coral Reef Protection Areas in Biscayne National Park. Popular diving destinations open to harvesting include Florida Keys locations outside prohibited areas, Miami-Dade County waters, Broward County reefs, and Palm Beach County diving spots. The 2026 mini season attracts thousands of recreational harvesters to these coastal locations.

Participants must possess a valid Florida saltwater fishing license, spiny lobster permit if required, approved measuring gauge, dive flag and proper safety equipment, and a cooler with ice for proper storage. According to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, spiny lobster mini season generates significant economic activity for coastal communities while supporting conservation efforts. The strict regulations, including size limits and seasonal restrictions, help maintain healthy lobster populations for both recreational and commercial harvesting.

cards.headline: Florida credit card holders take 12 months to pay off debt, ranking 30th nationwide
cards.teaser: Florida ranks in the middle of states for credit card payoff times, with residents carrying an average of $3,087 in debt and paying nearly $350 in interest charges.
cards.body:
Florida credit card holders are taking about a year to pay off their debt, according to a WalletHub study that placed the state 30th among states where it takes the longest to eliminate credit card balances. The typical Florida cardholder carries $3,087 in credit card debt and pays nearly $350 in interest charges while working to pay it off. The analysis found it takes the average Floridian 12 months to become debt-free from their credit cards.

The findings come as Americans nationwide are struggling with mounting credit card debt, with experts projecting total U.S. credit card debt will reach approximately $100 billion this year. For Florida families already dealing with rising costs of living, the data highlights the growing financial pressure many households face when managing everyday expenses on credit.

hero.headline: 100 animals rescued in worst hoarding case Martin County has ever seen, owners search for missing pets
hero.body:
Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. On Monday, authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and 5 more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs.

Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said about 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets. Every single one of them left in tears. The organization did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets. More identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

hero.headline: Three arrested in St. Lucie County death of 3-month-old who died from dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, face charges in the case.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect.

The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition. Each suspect faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement that the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office, and State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast home prices rise after two-year decline, with St. Lucie County up 2.3%
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after dropping from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down and they are probably going to continue to increase. She said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Decowski said buyers need to be realistic with their offers and need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and need to present a well-maintained product. For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans.

Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said this is going to be her family home as long as the market is still as high as it is. She said current prices are higher than she would hope for and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. Collins said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if they would be buying now. Condo and townhome prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Three arrested in death of 3-month-old from dehydration and malnutrition in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, who is Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, each face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect.

The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition. The sheriff's office said in a Facebook post that the arrests came after nearly a year of investigation by detectives and crime scene investigators working with the Medical Examiner's Office and state attorneys.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement that the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office and state attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to these arrests.

cards.headline: 100 animals rescued from Martin County hoarding case as owners search for missing pets
cards.teaser: Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered.
cards.body:
Authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property on Monday. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and 5 more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs. Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said about 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets. Unfortunately, every single one of them left in tears. They did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets. More identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

hero.headline: Three arrested in St. Lucie County death of 3-month-old who died from dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced the arrests in a Facebook post. Those facing charges are Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, who is Robert Maxwell's girlfriend.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Each suspect faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement that the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office, and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County sees highest home price increase on Treasure Coast, up 2.3% to $399,000
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Prices have dropped for condos and townhomes in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Florida spiny lobster mini season opens Wednesday for two-day harvest
hero.teaser: The annual spiny lobster sport season runs July 29-30, offering recreational divers and snorkelers two days to harvest the prized crustaceans under strict size and bag limits.
hero.body:
Florida's spiny lobster sport season runs Wednesday, July 29 through Thursday, July 30. The annual event occurs on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday of July each year, welcoming both Florida residents and non-residents to harvest spiny lobsters.

Bag limits vary by location. Monroe County and Biscayne National Park allow 6 lobsters per person per day, while the rest of Florida waters allow 12 lobsters per person per day. Possession limits off the water on July 29 equal the daily bag limit, but on July 30, harvesters may possess double the daily bag limit. All harvested spiny lobsters must have a carapace length exceeding 3 inches when measured in water, and possession of an approved measuring device is mandatory at all times.

Night diving is prohibited in Monroe County during the sport season only. Several areas remain closed to harvesting, including John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary no-take zones, Biscayne Bay/Card Sound Lobster Sanctuary, and five Coral Reef Protection Areas in Biscayne National Park. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission enforces the regulations to maintain healthy lobster populations for both recreational and commercial harvesting.

cards.headline: Florida credit card holders take 12 months to pay off debt, ranking middle nationwide
cards.teaser: Florida ranks 30th among states where it takes the longest to eliminate credit card balances, with the typical cardholder carrying $3,087 in debt.
cards.body:
Florida credit card holders are taking about a year to pay off their debt, according to a new WalletHub analysis that places the state 30th among states where it takes the longest to eliminate credit card balances. The typical Florida cardholder carries $3,087 in credit card debt and pays nearly $350 in interest charges while working to pay it off.

The analysis found it takes the average Floridian 12 months to become debt-free from their credit cards. Experts project total U.S. credit card debt will reach approximately $100 billion this year. For Florida families already dealing with rising costs of living, the data highlights the growing financial pressure many households face when managing everyday expenses on credit.

cards.headline: Health insurers reverse denials after media scrutiny, raising questions about approval process
cards.teaser: Florida patients denied coverage for cancer treatments, surgeries, and medications have seen denials reversed only after journalists began investigating their cases, with insurers offering no explanation for the sudden changes.
cards.body:
Since 2025, Florida patients denied insurance coverage for doctor-recommended procedures have had those denials reversed only after media scrutiny, with no explanation from insurers. Madeline Rogers of Zephyrhills was denied coverage for colon surgery three times, Mary Barnes, a breast cancer patient in St. Pete, was forced to halt chemotherapy treatments, and Broxley Bunt of West Palm Beach was denied coverage for surgery to remove a brain tumor. In each case, the denial was reversed only after reporting began.

United Healthcare reversed coverage for Barnes' breast cancer chemotherapy treatments after originally claiming her doctor-recommended treatments, which included immunotherapy, do not meet national cancer guidelines. The company then changed the designation to medically necessary. Dr. Bill Hennessey, a physician turned patient advocate, said denials are reversed when patients are correct and complain. Hennessey attributed the reversals to the power of the press, stating insurers do not want negative public relations.

Federal data recently analyzed by KFF found most health insurance claims are ultimately approved, but the data does not show how many claims are denied first since insurers only report the final outcome. Most patients who are denied never appeal. A spokesperson for AHIP, the nation's largest health insurance trade group, provided a statement but offered no specific explanation for why denials are reversed after media contact.
cards.article_text: HEALTH INSURANCE DENIALS AND "THE POWER OF THE PRESS"Since 2025, we've been investigating the cases of Florida patients denied insurance coverage for doctor-recommended procedures, including cancer treatments, medications and life-saving surgeries.In case after case, those denials were reversed only after we started asking questions, with no explanation from insurers.Watch report from Katie LagroneMadeline Rogers of Zephyrhills was denied coverage for colon surgery three times. Mary Barnes, a breast cancer patient in St. Pete, was forced to halt her chemotherapy treatments and Broxley Bunt of West Palm Beach was diagnosed with a brain tumor when he was denied coverage for surgery to get it removed.These are just a few of the stories we've shared as part of our ongoing, award-winning "Patient No More" series.DENIALS GET REVERSED WITH LITTLE TO NO EXPLANATIONBut in each case, the denial was reversed only after our reporting began — and even then, the insurance company offered no explanation for the sudden change."I was shocked. I was floored to hear from them so quickly," Rogers said after learning the $150,000 colon surgery would be covered after Investigative Reporter Kylie McGiven contacted Oscar Health about the denial."It's a relief, but why the hell do you have to go through this to get them to do what they're supposed to do to begin with?" Mary Barnes questioned after Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone told her United Healthcare would, in fact, cover her breast cancer chemotherapy treatments after they originally denied it.United originally claimed her doctor-recommended treatments, which included immunotherapy treatments, do not meet "national cancer guidelines" but then changed the designation to "medically necessary."REASONS FOR A DENIAL AND A SUBSEQUENT APPROVALDr. Bill Hennessey is a physician turned patient advocate who helps people appeal insurance denials and negotiate medical bills.He says most denials fall into three categories:Cost of care is too highA treatment isn't ‘medically necessary'Or a treatment is ‘experimental'When asked under what conditions most insurance companies reverse their denials, Hennessey was direct."It'll happen if, number one, you're right and number two, you complain," Hennessey said.As for why several denial cases we investigated ended up being reversed with no explanation, Hennessey summed it up like this: "Well, it's one of two things. You're either a miracle worker like Jesus, or you are correct. It is the power of the press. They don't want the negative public relations," Hennessey said.Federal data recently analyzed by KFF, the leading health policy organization in the U.S., found most health insurance claims are ultimately approved — but the data doesn't show how many claims are denied first, since insurers only report the final outcome.That's significant because most patients who are denied never appeal.Broxley Bunt was initially denied coverage for surgery to remove a meningioma brain tumor because his surgeon was out of network. His insurer, Florida Blue, reversed the denial after Reporter LaGrone started interviewing him from his hospital room where he underwent the surgery anyway."I don't think I could have done it on my own," Bunt said in response to the sudden reversal.Mark Armstrong recently got his blood cancer medication covered after his insurer, Oscar Health, wanted him to pay thousands of dollars up front as part of a "co-pay accumulator" policy."I HONESTLY BELIEVE IT'S BECAUSE YOU REACHED OUT TO THEM"But, according to a federal court ruling, Armstrong should have been exempt from this policy since the medication did not have a generic equivalent. LaGrone questioned Oscar about the exemption, and only then did the insurer make his medication available at no cost.His wife, Michele, believes the media scrutiny made all the difference."I honestly believe it's because you reached out to them. hero.headline: Three arrested in St. Lucie County death of 3-month-old who died from dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, who is Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, each face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office, and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

The sheriff's office said its responsibility is to pursue the truth, protect those who cannot protect themselves, and hold those responsible accountable. The investigation spanned nearly 12 months before the arrests were made Friday.

cards.headline: 100 animals rescued in Martin County hoarding case west of Hobe Sound, dozens search for missing pets
cards.teaser: Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast Friday morning hoping to be reunited with their missing animals.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has taken in 83 cats and 17 dogs from the property. Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, with 11 in cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

At 10 o'clock Friday morning, a line wrapped around the Humane Society building. About 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets, said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Every single one of them left in tears because the organization did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets. More identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

hero.headline: Indian River County home prices rise 1.8% as Treasure Coast housing market rebounds
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after price drops from 2023 to 2025. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Decowski said buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product, Decowski said. Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said this is going to be her family home as long as the market's still as high as it is.

Condo and townhome prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Collins said she wouldn't be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if her family would be buying now. Decowski said that means buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns Oct. 6 in Stuart to support youth mentoring programs
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties said the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: 3 arrested in death of 3-month-old in St. Lucie County who died from dehydration, malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, who is Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, face charges in the case.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Each suspect faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office, and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

cards.headline: 100 animals rescued in worst hoarding case Martin County has seen, owners search for missing pets
cards.teaser: Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning hoping to be reunited with their missing animals.
cards.body:
Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. On Monday, authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and 5 more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs.

Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said about 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets. She said every single one of them left in tears, and that they did not make a single identification. The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets, and more identification days are planned.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices climb after two years of declines
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after price drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices increased 1.1% since 2025 to $655,000. St. Lucie County saw the highest increase in the region at 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County increased 1.8% to a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that prices will come back down and they will probably continue to increase. She said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Decowski said buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product. For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell.

Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for and the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and afford a home for her kids if buying now. Condos and townhomes show a different trend. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County food and spirits fundraiser returns to Stuart in October
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

Organizers say the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: Florida spiny lobster mini season opens Wednesday with strict bag limits and prohibited zones
hero.teaser: Florida's spiny lobster sport season runs July 29-30, with different bag limits depending on location and strict regulations for recreational harvesters.
hero.body:
Florida's spiny lobster sport season returns Wednesday, July 29 through Thursday, July 30. The annual event occurs on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday of July each year, welcoming both Florida residents and non-residents. Bag limits vary by location, with Monroe County and Biscayne National Park allowing 6 lobsters per person per day, while the rest of Florida waters allow 12 lobsters per person per day. On the water, possession limits equal the daily bag limit. Off the water July 29, limits equal the daily bag limit, while off the water July 30, limits double to 12 or 24 depending on location.

All harvested spiny lobsters must meet Florida's minimum size requirement, with carapace length exceeding 3 inches when measured in water. Possession and use of an approved measuring device is mandatory at all times, and all measurements must be taken while the lobster is still in the water. Night diving is prohibited in Monroe County during sport season only, with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission defining diving as swimming at or below the water surface.

Several areas are closed to lobster harvesting, including John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary no-take zones, Biscayne Bay/Card Sound Lobster Sanctuary, and five Coral Reef Protection Areas in Biscayne National Park. Required equipment includes a valid Florida saltwater fishing license, spiny lobster permit, approved measuring gauge, dive flag and proper safety equipment, and a cooler with ice for proper storage.

cards.headline: Florida residents take 12 months on average to pay off credit card debt, new study finds
cards.teaser: Florida ranks 30th among states for longest credit card payoff times, with the typical cardholder carrying $3,087 in debt.
cards.body:
Florida credit card holders are taking about a year to pay off their debt, according to a new analysis from WalletHub that ranks the Sunshine State 30th among states where it takes the longest to eliminate credit card balances. The typical Florida cardholder carries $3,087 in credit card debt and pays nearly $350 in interest charges while working to pay it off.

The analysis found it takes the average Floridian 12 months to become debt-free from their credit cards. The findings come as Americans nationwide are struggling with mounting credit card debt. Experts project total U.S. credit card debt will reach approximately $100 billion this year.

Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product. For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. She would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and afford a home for her kids if buying now. Condos and townhomes tell a different story, with prices dropping in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increasing by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns to Stuart in October to support youth mentoring
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

The event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: 3 arrested in St. Lucie County after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday in St. Lucie County, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died from dehydration and malnutrition. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, each face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the child's grandparents brought the 3-month-old to the emergency room. Medical personnel notified the sheriff's office that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect.

The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition. The case required nearly a year of investigation before arrests were made.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership in the investigation. Del Toro said the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

hero.headline: Florida spiny lobster mini season opens July 29-30 with strict bag limits, prohibited zones
hero.teaser: Florida's two-day spiny lobster sport season returns Wednesday and Thursday with bag limits of 6 or 12 lobsters per person depending on location.
hero.body:
Florida's spiny lobster sport season runs Wednesday, July 29 through Thursday, July 30, offering recreational divers and snorkelers a two-day opportunity to harvest the crustaceans. The annual event occurs on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday of July each year, welcoming both Florida residents and non-residents. Monroe County and Biscayne National Park have a daily bag limit of 6 lobsters per person per day, while the rest of Florida waters allow 12 lobsters per person per day.

All harvested spiny lobsters must have a carapace length exceeding 3 inches when measured in water. Possession and use of an approved measuring device is mandatory at all times, and all measurements must be taken while the lobster is still in the water. Night diving is prohibited in Monroe County during sport season only, with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission defining diving as swimming at or below the water surface.

Several areas remain closed to lobster harvesting, including John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary no-take zones, Biscayne Bay/Card Sound Lobster Sanctuary, and five Coral Reef Protection Areas in Biscayne National Park. Harvesters must have a valid Florida saltwater fishing license, a spiny lobster permit if required, an approved measuring gauge, dive flag and proper safety equipment, and a cooler with ice for proper storage.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns to Stuart airport to support youth mentoring programs
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

According to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties, the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: Indian River County home prices rise 1.8% as Treasure Coast housing market rebounds
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after price drops from 2023 to 2025. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers. Buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

Prices for condos and townhomes have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Cara Collins, a Martin County homeowner who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell and would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and afford a home for her kids if buying now.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club building private racetrack resort community on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A new private racetrack resort community is under construction in St. Lucie County, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is being built on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road, replacing fairways with racing circuits and welcoming its first drivers this fall. The club features 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, said the club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, from kids as young as 8 years old driving go-karts to grandparents driving on track.

The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit. Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members.

Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks. Developers say they want to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5 million loss if property tax reform passes in November
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, forcing the department to consider closing stations or eliminating 116 firefighters.
cards.body:
County commissioners are set to discuss what those changes could mean for the fire department in a commission meeting Tuesday. Rick Sterl, president of the Martin County Firefighters Association, IAFF Local 2959, said most of the department's funding comes from the ad-valorem and general fund.

The proposed reform would increase the homestead exemption over two years. Martin County Fire Rescue's presentation outlines two stark options: cut services or cut staff. Cutting services would mean closing fire stations, ending hazmat, dive and technical rescue operations, grounding the critical care helicopter, and using firefighting equipment past its lifespan. Cutting staff would mean eliminating 116 firefighters over two years, roughly 1 in 3 of the firefighters in the department. Sterl said any reductions is going to possibly change the outcome of the level of care and the response time.

Residents in Martin County offered mixed reactions. Joe Vessichio said he does not believe the cuts will happen. Lisa Freitas, owner of Lisa Gay Fashions, said she is concerned about what cuts could mean for public safety. Fire rescue argues no version of the proposal allows the department to remain whole.

cards.headline: Martin County condo and townhome prices drop while single-family homes rise
cards.teaser: While single-family home prices are increasing across the Treasure Coast, prices for condos and townhomes have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties.
cards.body:
Prices have dropped for condos and townhomes in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. This contrasts with the single-family home market, where Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, St. Lucie County is up 2.3% since June 2025, and Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%.

The good news for buyers is that they are not seeing huge jumps in prices, Decowski said. However, Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down.

hero.headline: $16,000 Reward Offered as Murder Suspect Isabelle Johnson Remains at Large in Florida
hero.body:
The Walton County Sheriff's Office has announced a $16,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of Isabelle Johnson, 38, who is wanted on an open count of murder in connection with the death of Jason Coulthart. One month after Coulthart's remains were found buried on a Freeport property, investigators released new identifying details Friday in hopes of locating Johnson, who they believe has altered her appearance by cutting and dyeing her hair to avoid capture. The sheriff's office stated that Johnson is believed to have a rose or floral tattoo on her left hand extending from below her thumb toward her index finger, a tattoo on her right ankle, and a large scorpion tattoo stretching from her left buttock down her left thigh.

Coulthart, 43, was reported missing on May 24. His remains were discovered June 25 in a shallow grave on a property off Sunset Lane in Freeport after information developed during a Niceville Police Department missing persons investigation. Authorities later confirmed the remains belonged to Coulthart through DNA testing. The homicide investigation has already resulted in five arrests of individuals accused of helping Johnson evade law enforcement. Bobbi Wagstaff, 31, Martin Leaverton, 63, Sandra Leaverton, 63, Michael Ray White, 74, and Kathleen Morris, 59, have been charged with providing Johnson with shelter, transportation, supplies, cell phones or other assistance after Coulthart's death.

Investigators say Johnson is known to use multiple aliases, including Harley, Jessica Elaine Bowman, Jessica Elaine Thrush, Jessica Elaine Thrash, Jessica Dowdy, and possibly Denise. According to the sheriff's office, she often gains assistance by telling people she is fleeing domestic violence or facing other personal hardships. The Walton County Sheriff's Office emphasized that every lead is pursued, every tip is investigated, and that someone knows where she is.

The reward consists of $11,000 from Emerald Coast Crime Stoppers and the Florida Sheriffs Association Criminal Apprehension Assistance Program, with an additional $5,000 from the U.S. Marshals Task Force under separate reward guidelines. Anyone with information about Johnson's whereabouts is asked to contact the Walton County Sheriff's Office at 850-892-8111. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Emerald Coast Crime Stoppers by calling 850-863-TIPS (8477), online through Emerald Coast Crime Stoppers, or through the P3 Tips mobile app.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5M loss if property tax reform passes in November
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, forcing the department to choose between cutting services or eliminating 116 firefighters.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November. County commissioners are set to discuss what those changes could mean for the fire department in a commission meeting Tuesday. Rick Sterl, president of the Martin County Firefighters Association, IAFF Local 2959, said most of the department's funding comes from the ad-valorem and general fund.

The proposed reform would increase the homestead exemption over two years. Martin County Fire Rescue's presentation outlines two options: cut services or cut staff. Cutting services would mean closing fire stations, ending hazmat, dive and technical rescue operations, grounding the critical care helicopter, and using firefighting equipment past its lifespan. Cutting staff would mean eliminating 116 firefighters over two years, roughly 1 in 3 of the firefighters in their department.

Sterl said any reductions is going to possibly change the outcome of the level of care and the response time. Fire rescue argues no version of the proposal allows the department to remain whole. Residents in Martin County offered mixed reactions. Joe Vessichio said he does not believe the cuts will happen. Lisa Freitas, owner of Lisa Gay Fashions, said she is concerned about what cuts could mean for public safety.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and afford a home for her kids if her family were buying now.

Condos and townhomes show a different trend. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club building private racetrack resort on 650 acres in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A new private racetrack resort community is under construction off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits and welcoming its first drivers this fall.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is being built on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, said the club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, from 8-year-old kids driving go-karts to grandparents driving on track.

The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit. Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members.

Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

cards.headline: Families reunited with pets after 92 animals rescued from Hobe Sound property
cards.teaser: Families were reunited with their pets Wednesday at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast after animals were rescued from a Martin County property the sheriff described as the worst hoarding case it has ever seen.
cards.body:
The pets, 80 cats and 12 dogs, were rescued from a property located in the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle, west of Hobe Sound, on Monday. Investigators said the home belongs to 77-year-old Gail Giustino. Sheriff John Budensiek said Wednesday was emotional for families who had feared they would never see their animals again.

Linh Nguyen had been searching for her cat Patchy since January. She said she cried so much when she lost him and there were many nights when she could not sleep. She said she was praying to God and asking for a miracle, and when she saw the news on Monday night, she had a very strong feeling. The sheriff's office said a microchip made the reunion possible.

Lori Tucker, the shelter's director of operations, said it is important that the animals are reunited with the correct owners. Anyone who believes their pet may be among those rescued is asked to first file a lost pet report with the Martin County Sheriff's Office. From there, an appointment can be made with the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast.
